rv.q: Above all else, it is fun - and that is one thing Toronto theatregoers have in common with mysterious Jazz Age millionaires: sometimes, we all just want to have a good time.
The show is one of the most lavish I've ever seen in a touring production.
With some reservations, this musical production of The Great Gatsby can be recommended for those individuals who are looking for something different.
Sadly, the five-star production values are wrapped around a barely two-star adaptation of the novel itself.
Indeed, despite its pedigree, the glittery North American touring production is an only so-so proposition.
The Great Gatsby is polished, energetic, visually exciting, and led by an exceptional company.

There’s more than enough going for this production that, if you’re a fan of the novel and lavish musicals, Old Sport, you should have no reservations about following that green light that so obsesses Jay Gatsby all the way to Playhouse Square.
Its over-the-top grandiosity is the best feature of “The Great Gatsby."
Honestly, this "Gatsby” rivals another recent extravaganza, “Moulin Rouge,” for thrilling artistic spectacle.
But the storytelling falls short of the novel’s genius, and in so doing misses a remarkable opportunity to say something meaningful about our current moment in American history.
It's a glossy — and, to be clear, often entertaining — reimagining that ignores most of the key themes of the text.
Have fun going for the glitter, but you won’t find much of the gold of Fitzgerald’s stellar vision and voice.

This musical adaptation does not meet that high bar.

While visually stunning and brimming with high-caliber talent, The Great Gatsby musical struggled to translate the novel's narrative into a compelling stage experience on Wednesday night at the Music Hall at Fair Park.
But the musical flattens the story’s ironies and paradoxes into a standard-issue tragic romance, one that doesn't do justice to either Jay or Daisy.
The Broadway tour at the Orpheum dazzles the eye but squanders the soul of an American classic.
But in the end, it seems to be about nothing so much as Jay Gatsby’s (Jake David Smith) parties and what they wore—and that is simply not enough to merit two-and-a-half hours of stage time.
The shapeless, dumbed-down mishmash at the Citizens Opera House is not.
Even on second thought, the show is dreadful.

cn.t: Lavish production values and stunning costumes dazzle, but critics find this adaptation sacrifices Fitzgerald's darker themes for spectacle and romance, resulting in a visually opulent yet dramatically shallow take on the classic novel.
